document.abstract: Southwestern Bell Telephone (SWBT) Technology Planning chose a digital fiber-optic, integrated narrowband/broadband fiber-to-the-curb (FTTC) access architecture for deployment in the Richardson, Texas, video trial. The trial architecture consists of a two-level network: Level 1 and Level 2. The Level-1 network is the infrastructure provided by SWBT. The Level-2 network is that portion which provides the digital video services and the analog broadcast services. This paper describes the network designed for SWBT that will be used to replace and extend the existing telephony transport and access network in Richardson with a state-of-the-art network that will provide telephony and other narrowband services, analog broadcast video services, digital broadcast services, and interactive switched digital video services. Also discussed are some of the new operations, administration, maintenance, and provisioning systems (OAM&P) required in this new environment. The characteristics and challenges of this new network, new technology, and the Richardson video trial are examined in detail.

authors.bio: Michele Kerr is corporate manager, technology planning, at SBC Communications, Inc., in St. Louis, Mo. She graduated from the University of Arkansas with a B.S.C.E. Following graduation she joined Southwestern Bell Telephone in 1977, where she has worked as an outside plant engineer and an outside plant engineering manager. After joining the SWBT headquarters staff, Kerr was responsible for the development and implementation of company-wide engineering methods and procedures, including policies for the deployment of fiber-optic cable, digital loop carrier, and SONET multiplexing equipment. As the network architect for the Richardson video trial, she is responsible for defining network requirements, standardizing network elements and design criteria, developing functional specifications, and resolving technical issues. She is also responsible for monitoring the network costs and ensuring the most economical architecture to meet the service needs.
authors.name: Michele Kerr

authors.bio: Russ Couture holds a B. S. degree from the University of Massachusetts and a master's degree in science from Northeastern University. He has been with Bell Laboratories for 33 years, first in North Andover, Mass., and now in Holmdel, N. J. He has been a lead architectural manager for Southwestern Bell Telephone for full-service switched digital video broadband/narrowband in Richardson, Tex. He defined and documented the original network requirements and the architecture to support them, working closely with SWBT to analyze service needs and to assure consistency with Lucent Technologies' platform strategy. Couture worked with a multi-company team to identify and resolve technical issues regarding Richardson implementation and was a core member in the effort to define signaling and control protocols and systems. He also chaired the technical change control team that manages the product and architecture functional or pricing changes. Prior to his work on the Richardson video trial, Russ was responsible for applications and economic modeling of DACS II and DACS III and IV-2000. He is a member of the IEEE and Communications Society and of the Society of Cable Telecommunication Engineers.
authors.name: Russ Couture

authors.bio: Douglas Ramsayer holds an M. B. A. from the University of North Carolina and an undergraduate degree from Kenyon College. His six years of experience in the telecommunications industry covers fiber optics, broadband networks, and network management systems. Currently, Ramsayer is the product line manager for Applied Digital Access in San Diego, Calif. At the time this paper was written, he was with BroadBand Technologies, Inc., in Research Triangle Park, N. C.
authors.name: Douglas Ramsayer

authors.bio: Joe Rich graduated from the University of Arkansas with B. S. E. E. and M. S. E. E. degrees in biomedical engineering, communications, and electromagnetics. Currently senior staff engineer at Lockheed Martin Telecommunications, he joined Lockheed in 1979 and has worked on several satellite and ground communication programs. As part of a 1985 Independent Research and Development project, he helped to develop a subband tuner and 256 voice grade channel fdm demultiplexer using FFTs, and demonstrated an 18 Gbit/sec packet switch. Rich was the systems engineer responsible for developing and implementing the digital interface between the satellite ground terminals and signal processing equipment at several major government communication facilities and helped to define and develop a fiberoptic ATM-based satellite communication bus. He served as system architect on the Southwestern Bell Richardson Video Project.
authors.name: Joe Rich
